newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish premier Bruton urges credible IRA truce.
newsitem.headline: Irish premier Bruton urges credible IRA truce.

text.p: Irish Prime Minister John Bruton said on Wednesday that IRA guerrillas could be represented at Northern Ireland peace talks in January if the outlawed group called a new ceasefire "in words that are believable".

Bruton acknowledged that his understanding of how the Irish Republican Army's political wing, Sinn Fein, could enter talks differed from Britain's, but said he hoped to iron out differences in talks with British Prime Minister John Major in London on Monday.

The Irish leader said that if the IRA called a credible ceasefire and Sinn Fein adhered to democratic rules governing the talks, the guerrillas could be represented at the Belfast peace talks after the Christmas recess.

Major said last week that Britain would first have to be satisfied that any new IRA truce was credible. In February the guerrillas ended a 17-month ceasefire in their war against British rule of Northern Ireland.

But Bruton said his government opposed any rewriting of the rules the two countries had worked out to convene the most serious attempt in 27 years to negotiate a settlement between pro-British Unionists and Irish nationalists.

"This means that if the IRA clearly called an unequivocal ceasefire, in words that are believable, and provided there is an adherence to the Mitchell principles, then Sinn Fein should be admitted to the talks," he told Ireland's parliament.

The five-month-old talks, chaired by former U.S. senator George Mitchell, group all the province's major political parties except Sinn Fein in an attempt to end a conflict which has killed 3,200 in the past quarter century.
Mitchell wrote a series of democratic principles which commit parties to accepting the outcome of the talks and shunning violence.

Sinn Fein is barred from the talks since the IRA ended its ceasefire and Major has said the guerrillas will have to prove any new truce is not a tactical ploy by calling a halt to targetting and surveillance.
Bruton said one of the reasons mediation efforts by peace-broker John Hume appeared to be deadlocked was a lack of trust between the IRA and the British government.

"It is for this reason that both governments are engaged in intensive contact with a view to developing our respective positions. That work will be continued in the days before Monday's Anglo-Irish summit," he said.
"Unless both governments are travelling together on the same road towards the same destination, progress is simply not possible," he said.
Hume leads the moderate Irish nationalist Social, Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) and is engaged in behind-the-scenes moves to secure a new IRA truce by Christmas.
Bruton's statement was seen as a further push at the Irish Republican Army to call an end to its current bombing campaign, which has seen attacks in Britain, Germany and Northern Ireland.
